sections.title: Perspicax console: Data access (Accès aux données)
sections.where: Perspicax console > Access (Accès) > Data access (Accès aux données) (/access/data)
sections.text: Accès > Accès aux données (`/access/data`, spec 2026-10-13 section 8 / 9.7): rules that block or allow-only entities for a role, person or service account (bot), a live preview of what a user sees, and the policy's audit history. Admins only. Client groups are out of scope for this version (DAP-6): no groups tab.

sections.title: Perspicax console: Keys (Clés)
sections.text: `/credentials`: the one place every key is managed (JC, 2026-09-29: "une page pour gérer les credentials à un seul endroit"). Two pills since lot 8 of the Cursor style (2026-10-18, R03 Personal / SSH): Clés de produit and, while a Sagax server is linked, Clés de modèle (the person's own model keys for Sagax, their one place, doublon 1). The product keys are a light table (R03, R26): the name (renamed in place) over its description, the product or family, the type in a pill, the key masked to its last four ("...wdtx"), who uses it, the expiry with its tone, the last use, the owner by avatar and "…". One funnel filters by product or family, type, owner and state (its facets in use show as chips); a checkbox column carries the bulk expiry and the bulk delete. Products that still have no key are a banner above the table, and a key's usage is a link of its "…". A product key is an exact product id (`cw_cpq`) or a covering group (`cw_psa_*`). A key shared by a whole family is drawn once and its product cell says the family ("ConnectWise PSA").

sections.title: Perspicax console: Flow
sections.text: The Flow page (`/flow`, docs/flow-actions.md): the signed packs of the host (stage from local files, activate, roll back, delete one that is not active), the profile to tenant links, the host settings read only (they come from the environment, never from the console) and a dry run of one action with its render. Admins only; a host without Flow configured answers `flow_not_configured` and the page says so.

sections.title: Perspicax console: To do (À traiter)
sections.where: Perspicax console > To do (À traiter) > To do (À traiter) (/inbox)
sections.text: À traiter (`/inbox`; lot A, redrawn as an inbox on 2026-10-11, JC: "Maybe the Todo should be more like an Inbox"). Since lot 9 of the Cursor style (2026-10-18, spec 5.3, R28): the folders (À faire, Plus tard, Fait) are pills, the type a menu beside the search, the list takes the page's width (what, who, since when; bold until opened) and an item opens in the detail panel on the right (Mis en forme / Brut, J and K, Escape), the whole screen on a phone. Nothing open, no panel. What arrives: the requests of the person's Sagax bots (while a server is linked), the memory proposals they review (managers), the questions a colleague asked them through ask_person (everyone), and for an admin the failed routines of the last seven days (Sagax incidents), the platform's alerts (Accueil's health reasons, a bot server not heard from) and the writes the memory's filter refused in the last 30 days (the old Quarantaine page). Lot F (2026-10-17, JC: "À traiter keeps its state in the URL"; one approvals queue): the folder, the type, the view, the search (live) and the open item are the address (`?folder=&type=&view=&q=&item=`), so a reload, a shared link or Back restores the view; the order is fixed per folder (`lib/inbox.ts`). The old approvals page (`/sagax/approvals`) and the old Propositions page (`/memory/proposals`) redirect here: an admin reads the organization's requests (`view=org`), the decided ones are a tab of the bots' journal; a proposal is reviewed in full in the reader (edit, merge, refuse, return), the safe ones approved in bulk, and an author reads their own (`view=mine`). « Fait » holds every type: what was answered here, what was set aside, what the server settled. J and K walk the list, E marks done, Escape closes the open item.

sections.title: Perspicax console: Journal
sections.text: `/journal`, the one Journal (2026-10-18, Cursor style, spec section 5.10, R28): « Tout ce qui s'est passé, qui l'a fait et avec quel résultat. » An admin picks the source in pills, Passerelle (the gateway's five tables, the default), Bots (the linked Sagax server's journals) and Mémoire (the memory audit); a manager reads the Passerelle source alone. Inside a source the « Vue » menu picks the table (`?view=`), a row opens the detail panel, and the page head's « ... » copies the link and exports. The old addresses land here, their query kept (`main.tsx`): the tables' own paths (`/journal/vendor` is `?view=vendor`), an old `?tab=`, the Sagax logs (`/sagax/logs` is `?source=bots`) and the memory journal (`/memory/journal` is `?source=memory`). The Passerelle source opens on the traffic charts that were Accueil's (volume in and out, bottlenecks).

sections.title: Perspicax console: My profile (Mon profil)
sections.where: Perspicax console > My account (Mon compte) > My profile (Mon profil) (/me)
sections.text: Réglages › Compte (lot 4 of the Cursor-style console, spec 5.11 and doublon 22, R19): one's own photo, name and coordinates, the one place they are edited. The page reads as rows, the label at the left and the value in grey, a « Modifier » at the right of the identity row; that button opens the form as an inner step of the window with its own Enregistrer (Escape or Annuler leaves the step, not the window). The photo applies at once (its own crop sheet). `/me` is the profile others see, read only, and its « Modifier » opens this page. Lot 6 of the Cursor-style console: « Supprimer mon compte » (Loi 25, `POST /api/v1/me/erase`, docs/account-deletion.md) is the last row, alone under its own heading, away from the benign rows (S5). It opens an inner step that says what goes and what stays, asks the proofs the server asks (the current password, the authenticator code, or for a passkey-only account a sign-in of the last ten minutes) and the login typed again; the button stays disabled until it matches. Irreversible: the session ends with the account and the page goes to the sign-in screen. The one place for it: an admin erases another person from that person's sheet.

sections.title: Perspicax console: My journal (Mon journal)
sections.where: Perspicax console > My account (Mon compte) > My journal (Mon journal) (/me/journal)
sections.text: One's own activity, at the head of Mon profil (lot 6 of the Cursor-style console, spec 5.13, R01 and R13): four figures (calls of 30 days, distinct tools of 30 days, the longest streak, the current one), the ActivityHeatmap of 53 weeks with its legend and the busiest month and day, and the tools used most. Mon journal (`/me/journal`) keeps the rows. Real data only. Every figure is the journal summary of the person's own MCP calls (`GET /api/v1/me/journal/requests/summary`), counted by the server over the whole window, not the newest rows of a list: the year in four windows of at most 91 days, each cut in days from a local midnight (the summary keeps a bucket per day up to 100 days, from `from`; a day that crosses a change of hour is an hour off at its edge). What the journal no longer keeps (its retention, Réglages › Système) counts as nothing, and the page says so; the bots' turns and the console's own actions are not MCP calls and are not counted here.

sections.title: Perspicax console: Notes
sections.text: The live preview editor of Mémoire > Notes (`/memory/notes`, 2026-10-12; JC: "100% des notes doivent être éditables tel que Obsidian"): one CodeMirror 6 editor per note, no read mode and no edit mode. The markdown is drawn as it reads (headings sized, bold and italic, lists with their bullet, checkboxes that toggle, links and [[wikilinks]] as links, code and quotes) and shown as source on the lines the cursor is on, Obsidian's live preview. `[[` opens the readable notes, Enter inserts the link; Cmd or Ctrl+click follows a link; Cmd or Ctrl+S saves now. Loaded in its own chunk by the notes page only (look amendment section 30). The markdown grammar is `@lezer/markdown` with GFM; the look is `theme` below, on the console's tokens, so it rides in this chunk.

sections.title: Perspicax console: Quality (Qualité)
sections.text: The measures section of the Quality page (`/memory/quality`, below the lists of lot A.5; lot A.8 of the 2026-10-09 master plan; analysis 17.16, 17.17, 17.25; measure doc section 7): is the memory worth it? The pursue criterion and the card stop rule (decision 13), evaluated by the gateway, their reasons rendered from their numbers; tokens per turn, cards used, hints and the work they avoided, contested facts; the weekly cross-person duplicates next to the A.0 baseline; the detector's settings in one line, set in Réglages › Mémoire (`detector.tsx`, lot 4 doublon 12). Counts only, never a person. Admins only.

sections.title: Perspicax console: Tags (Étiquettes)
sections.text: Étiquettes of the Mémoire section (`/memory/tags`, lot A.2; plan 2026-10-09-memory-tiers-plan.md, slice 6), admins only: the tag namespaces (a manual vocabulary, or one synced from a served API through a directory person's read access), their values, their sync; the teams left out of the org directory and its rebuild. Lot A.5 moved the review settings to Politiques (with the namespaces required on shared writes) and added a search over the namespaces. Lot 4 of the Cursor-style console (doublon 11): a namespace's « requis » is read here and set in Réglages › Mémoire only.

sections.access: managers only; shown while a Sagax server is linked
sections.text: A manager's Accueil (`/sagax`; lot 6 of the Cursor-style console, spec 5.2 and doublon 28, R01 and R02): the bots' overview of 2026-10-08 in the template of every Accueil. « Bienvenue, <prénom>. »; the banner of a new version; one banner per thing that needs attention (an approval waiting, a failed routine, an engine missing or failing, errors, a low disk, a failed backup), each leading where the fix is; « Activité »: the turns of 30 days with their bars per day, the active bots, the cost of 30 days and the approvals; the À traiter card beside the most active bots; the product cards. What every Sagax serves gives these figures (`GET bots`, `GET usage`, `GET approvals`); a newer Sagax also reports its health (`GET overview`, offered in `GET capabilities`), which only feeds the banners. No figure is made up. The engines table, the host and the server's facts left (doublons 3 and 6: Réglages › Bots, Moteurs et outils). An admin's Accueil is `/status`: `/sagax` lands there (`main.tsx`).

sections.title: Perspicax console: Bots
sections.access: managers and admins; shown while a Sagax server is linked
sections.text: The Bots page of the Sagax section (`/sagax/bots`, `/sagax/bots/:id`, 2026-10-08; until then the Robots tab of Utilisateurs et équipes): every bot of the linked server, a row opening the bot's sheet; its tab Fichiers (`/sagax/files`) browses a bot's files. Slice b of the design gives a bot its own page and the actions. Lot 9 of the Cursor style (2026-10-18, spec 5.4, R02, R07): one bar for both views, the state in pills (Tous, Actifs, Archivés), the search and the funnel of owners and engines, the Galerie / Liste switch in icons at the right; the address keeps them (`?state=&q=&owner=&engine=&view=`).

sections.title: Perspicax console: Computers (Ordinateurs)
sections.access: admins only; shown while a Sagax server is linked
sections.text: The computers of a linked Sagax (`/sagax/computers`, admins, 2026-10-12): every server environment (the organization's machine for one person, sagax-sandboxd) and every desktop signed in to the server (the person's own computer, listed read only). The environments' facts sit on top (configured, reachable, how many may run, the idle stop); each row says its owner, kind, state, CPU and memory, workspace against its quota (over quota warns), image or system, last use and the bots that work there. A row opens a sheet with the detail, the recent activity and the actions the computer offers now (`actions[]`), each behind a confirmation: reset and delete with the name typed, and a busy computer's confirmation says a bot works there. A desktop has no action, and the sheet says why. Sagax's refusals read in words. A Sagax that does not serve the computers says so.

sections.title: Perspicax console: Engines and tools (Moteurs et outils)
sections.where: Perspicax console > Connections (Connexions) > Engines and tools (Moteurs et outils) (/sagax/connections)
sections.access: admins only; shown while a Sagax server is linked
sections.text: The Engines and tools page of the Sagax section (`/sagax/connections`, 2026-10-08, slice d of docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-08-sagax-admin-console-design.md, section 4.6; Cursor style lot 8, 2026-10-18, R14 and R15): what the linked Sagax connects to, admins only. Four pills, each a ConnectedList (what works, then what does not): Engines (the image's engines, the organization key, whether the policies allow it), MCP servers (organization and personal, with Composio as one card), Skills (the organization library) and Marketplaces. The People tab of before moved to the person's sheet (their engines are there). A Test button asks Sagax to check one line now (`POST connections/test`); per-person checks are never computed in the background, and a stdio MCP server's test answers 501 with a reason, shown as Sagax wrote it. Which engines and marketplaces are allowed is set in Réglages › Bots › Politiques only (doublons 3 and 5): here a pill and a link.

sections.title: Perspicax console: Bot rights (Droits sur les bots)
sections.where: Perspicax console > Access (Accès) > Bot rights (Droits sur les bots) (/sagax/permissions)
sections.access: admins only; shown while a Sagax server is linked
sections.text: The « Qui a quoi » tab of the Permissions page (`/sagax/permissions?tab=assign`, 2026-10-09, migration 0051): who holds which permission set, built for hundreds of people. People or teams (`?who=`), a search, a filter by team and by set, 50 rows per page. A person's row lists their own sets and, muted, the sets their teams give them. Everyone holds the default set: it is named once above the table. One at a time, a set is given on the person's sheet (Bots) or on the team's page (Bots), and each row leads there. In bulk (lot 9, JC's decision of 2026-10-18: this view is the one place for it), the rows' boxes and the bar « Donner / Retirer » a set: the confirmation names exactly who changes (and who already is as asked), the change is sent once (`POST /api/v1/pulsabot/permission-sets/{id}/assign|unassign`, audited), then the assignments are read again and the result says, per person or team, what holds now. The engines the organization's accounts serve (voice mode, avatars, Grok: migration 0067, 2026-10-19, JC: « assigner ça de masse et par équipe ») are given here the same way: their column shows each row's own engines and, muted, those its teams give; the bar picks one or more engines, the confirmation names who changes and who already holds them through a team, one call (`POST /api/v1/pulsabot/server-engines/assign|unassign`, audited) and the rows read again. A person's own engines also stay on their sheet.

sections.title: Perspicax console: Routines
sections.access: every person of the organization; shown while a Sagax server is linked
sections.text: The routines calendar of the Sagax section (`/sagax/routines`, 2026-10-12), Sagax's Automations calendar in the console: every run of a window, past and planned (`GET routines/runs`), drawn on a week of hours by days (the default), on a month, or kept as the list of routines (the table of slice c, managers). Each run is a block colored by its state (ok, failed, skipped, running; a planned run is dashed); a run outside the caller's reach comes redacted and shows as an anonymous block. The scope is Moi, Équipe or Tous as the role allows (a scope Sagax refuses with `routine_scope_not_allowed` is hidden); the bot, the state and the search narrow the runs. A run opens a sheet with its facts, its reason, its thread in Sagax and its routine's actions (Run now, Pause, Resume, managers and admins). On the phone the week is a day agenda, like Sagax iOS: the days in a strip, the chosen day's runs as rows.

sections.text: `/settings/service-accounts`: bot accounts that authenticate with a minted `pxat1.` token instead of signing in. `POST /api/v1/users` with `kind: "service"` forces `role: "employee"` server side regardless of what is sent (a bot manages nothing), so this page never offers a role picker.

The traffic charts moved to Journal (Passerelle) and the sessions tile left (doublon 18: the count is Journal › Sessions').

sections.title: Perspicax README.md: Access control
sections.text:
- Profiles. A profile names a set of products and, per product, what is
 exposed (tags, methods, operations, the fields a write may set), the
 serving mode (`model`, `compact`, `minimal`, `group`, `hybrid`,
 `per_operation`) and the writes held for a confirmation. Holding a profile is what a token grants; two profiles on one
 product stay exactly separated per caller, including in discovery.
- Credentials. Vendor secrets are `{ env: NAME }` or `{ file: path }` refs in
 `apis.yaml`, or sealed in the vault (XChaCha20-Poly1305) under the gateway.
 They never appear in a log, a tool result or an error message. An empty
 variable or a whitespace only file counts as missing, and `check` says so.
 Auth strategies: `none`, `api_key`, `bearer`, `basic`,
 `oauth2_client_credentials`, `oauth2_authorization_code` (the runtime only
 ever refreshes; the console starts the vendor dance), `token_login`,
 `web_session` and `cw_manage` (the four Manage slots).
- Key assignment. On Affectation, a checked box means this key is linked
 to that profile. A profile already served by another key of the same family
 has no checkbox. It is listed under "Already served by another key", with
 the name of the key that serves it ("This key is not linked to it. Served
 by {name}."). Removing the key from a product removes every binding that
 covers that product, not only the row the resolver picks. Removing a
 product from a profile also drops key bindings left with nothing to serve
 for that product (`docs/releases/1.8.13.md`).
- Key deletion. Deleting a key drops its profile links, its person links
 and the product defaults it carries. Deletion is refused only while a
 product header, query or var still seals the value. The refusal says
 "A product still seals this value." The store schema stays at 46. Rows
 already stored stay as they are until a key is deleted or a product is
 removed from a profile.
- Vault key rotation, offline only. Stop the connector, then run
 `pulsatrix-connector gateway rotate-vault`: it refuses while a connector
 holds the config directory (`state/serve.lock`) and while the store holds a
 sealed row it cannot re-seal, writes the new key to `state/vault.key.next`,
 re-seals every live sealed table (credentials, TOTP secrets, MCP headers,
 web sessions, email secrets, OIDC signing keys, Sagax owner model keys)
 in one transaction, and only then keeps the old key as
 `state/vault.key.prev`. Under the `env` provider it prints the new
 `PXC_VAULT_KEY` value and waits for its fingerprint. The Status page shows
 the key's source, version and fingerprint.
- Route roles. Every `/api/v1` route has a declared minimum role
 (`crates/gateway/tests/route_roles.rs`), checked against its handler and
 against a live refusal.
- A local OAuth 2.1 server. An MCP client registers (a Client ID Metadata
 Document, or Dynamic Client Registration as the fallback), runs PKCE with
 `resource` bound to the `/mcp` audience, and the user signs in with a password

sections.title: Perspicax README.md: Deploy
sections.text:
| Path | What |
 
| `deploy/Dockerfile` | the image: a Rust build stage, then the release binary on `debian:trixie-slim`, an unprivileged user, the config directory as a volume, `pulsatrix-connector healthz` as the health check (liveness). `GET /readyz` is the probe that withholds traffic when the store does not answer. `make image` builds and tags it |
| `docker-compose.yml` | local stack: `docker compose up` from the repository root. SQLite lives on the config volume, so there is no separate database |
| `.env.example` | the process environment the binary and the compose files read, with empty placeholders |
| `.github/workflows/ci.yml` | started by hand (`workflow_dispatch`): format, clippy, tests, the console checks, and an image build. The local gate is `make ci`. GitHub Actions does not run on push or pull request |
| `deploy/docker-compose.traefik.yml` | Traefik with Let's Encrypt in front of the container |
| `deploy/Caddyfile` | Caddy on the same host, automatic certificate, SSE friendly proxy settings, with its own compose file |
| `deploy/README.md` | first run in a container, `/healthz` vs `/readyz`, backups, the signed archive format |
| `infra/` | the Azure path: a Bicep template (Arm64 VM, managed disk for the store, ACR, Key Vault, a public IP with 80 and 443 only), the build and push scripts, and the Caddy plus Perspicax compose that runs on it |
The binary speaks plain HTTP on `bind` and expects TLS to terminate at an edge
that sets `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto`; `public_origin` is what that
edge exposes and every OAuth issuer and audience derives from it.

sections.title: Perspicax README.md: How it is tested
sections.text:
Every layer below ran on the 1.5.0 release branch before the tag; the numbers
are recorded in `AGENTS.md`.
| Layer | What it checks | 1.5.0 |
 
| `make check` | `cargo fmt --check`, `clippy -D warnings`, `cargo test` over every crate (real `wiremock` vendors and real files, no mocks), `cargo outdated`, the toolchain | 1184 passed, 0 failed, 6 ignored over 123 test targets; fmt, clippy, outdated and toolchain clean |
| `make console-check` | TypeScript, the design tokens, every i18n key present in both languages and used | clean, 1521 keys |
| `make console-e2e` | Playwright against a connector the suite starts, including the phone-width gate at 390 px | 100 passed, 26 skipped, 0 failed |
| `make eval-replay` | every task's reference calls through every surface variant, no model | 24 of 24 held-out and 36 of 36 original on the five variants, 0 tool errors |
| `make eval` | a real small model over the fake vendor (above) | `group` 90.3%, `hybrid` 90.3%, `compact` with its guide 91.7%, against 44.4% for 1.4.0 |
| `make image` | the container builds, and started the way `docker-compose.yml` starts it, seeds its config and turns healthy | 212 MB, Docker health status `healthy` |
| Reviews | an independent verification pass of the small-model work, and a review of each of the ten pull requests merged into this release | 23 confirmed findings fixed with a test each (among them a recipe that read `_dry_run: "true"` as false and sent the write, `.` and `..` accepted as an id, two profiles on one product locked out of `per_operation` by each other); merging one pull request's tests found a real defect, fixed: a `web_session` caller never hit the strategy cache and reloaded its cookie jar on every call |
| Real tenants | no write during development | no agent called the operator's configured Perspicax MCP connectors while this was built; every write of every evaluation went to the fake vendor |

sections.title: Perspicax README.md: Measured with a small local model
sections.text:
Version 1.5.0 asked one question: can a model small enough to run on one
workstation pick the right ConnectWise tool and call it correctly? It was
measured, not assumed.
- Model. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, quantised UD-Q4_K_XL, on llama-server with
 thinking on, temperature 0.6, four slots of 131,072 tokens and at most ten
 turns per task, on an Apple M3 Max.
- Vendor. An invented ConnectWise Manage
 (`evals/small-model/fakevendor/`): a
 fictitious Quebec MSP served over the committed `cw_psa_*` catalogs. No
 real tenant, no real data, no key.
- Tasks. 24 held-out requests a technician or a dispatcher would type,
 written blind to the surfaces: simple and filtered reads, sub resources,
 multi-step reads, sums, notes, updates, creates, time entries, and traps

sections.title: Perspicax README.md
Perspicax README.md: Quick start
sections.text:
The config directory is `--config-dir`, else `PXC_CONFIG_DIR`, else
`~/.config/pulsatrix-connector`, created `0700`. `init` never asks for or writes
a secret. Between `import` and `check`, edit `apis.yaml`: give the API its
`base_url` and `auth`, and an `expose` block (mandatory above 100 operations).
Importing something other than a starter catalog:
 
A catalog imported from a URL is checked again on a schedule: five minutes
after boot, then every `catalog_refresh_hours` (a setting, 24 by default, `0`
turns it off), the connector fetches the URL, compares the document's hash with
the active version and stages a changed one as a pending version for an admin
to review and activate from the catalog screen. Nothing is swapped by the
schedule. The same screen has a "check the source now" button and a changelog
tab listing what every swap added, removed or changed.
Vendor documents come from the private
`pulsatrixtechnologies/pulsatrix-sources` repository, one folder per product
with a README that says where the document comes from and what its compiled
surface looks like. Public documents are fetched with the `curl` line in that
README; login walled ones are downloaded from the vendor portal by the operator.
Adding a product end to end is
`docs/api-onboarding-recipe.md`.
Guides are installed by hand, with one exception. Two starter guides ship
under `catalog/guides/`, in the release archive and inside
the binary: `cw_psa.guide.json` for the twelve Manage modules (with twelve
recipes), installed by hand, and `sentinelone.guide.json`, which folds
SentinelOne's model view into its compact one and is marked
`"install": "auto"`. The connector seeds that one itself, once, at boot or
reload, into a config dir that has the `sentinelone` catalog imported and no
guide by that id; it records the seed in `state/guides_seeded.json`, and under
the gateway in the audit log as `guide.seed`. Removing it is permanent: the
connector never seeds it again.
 
`import` refuses a guide that names a resource or a field the catalogs do not
have, or that is over its budget, and prints the budget line; `api_reload` or
a restart serves it. Under the gateway, the product page's Guide panel does
the same: upload a guide, or install the starter guide that covers the
product. An upgrade past the SentinelOne literal needs no step of its own:
the first boot seeds `sentinelone.guide.json`. `check` warns about any API
whose model view lists more than 150 tools with no guide folding it.
Serving mode, time and confirmation in `apis.yaml` and `config.toml`:
 
Write-approval rules for a bot account live in ` /write_approvals.yaml` (copy `docs/write-approvals.yaml`; see `docs/mcp-surface.md`, Write approvals). A listed account may write only when a rule matches; there is no alwaysAllow; a match waits 15 minutes for `review_write`.

sections.title: Perspicax README.md: What it does
sections.text:
Perspicax is a standalone Rust server, run as `pulsatrix-connector`. It reads
the API document a vendor already publishes and serves that vendor as MCP tools
over Streamable HTTP, behind its own OAuth 2.1 server. Four steps:
1. Import a document. `pulsatrix-connector import` takes an OpenAPI 3 or
 Swagger 2 document, a ReDoc HTML bundle, an authored RPC method file, a
 GraphQL introspection result, or another MCP server's tool list read over the
 protocol. The file (or `https://` URL) is stored in the Perspicax config
 directory; nothing vendor specific lives in the repository or in the binary.
2. Compile a catalog. The compiler normalizes the document into a catalog
 plus a resource model: path families become resources with verbs, identity
 fields, references, sub resources and actions. The format is
 `docs/catalog-format.md`. A recompile of an
 unchanged document is byte identical.
3. Serve MCP tools. Per catalog the client sees one ` __query` tool, one
 ` __ _write` tool per writable resource, and an action tool for
 each leftover operation. `mode: compact` folds the writes and actions into
 ` __write` and ` __action`; `mode: minimal` serves the query tool
 alone; `mode: group` serves the members of a registry group (the twelve
 `cw_psa_*` Manage modules) through three tools, `cw_psa__query`,
 `cw_psa__write` and `cw_psa__action`; `mode: hybrid` adds a guide's
 recipes, one tool per common task. Meta-tools sit beside them: `api_list`,
 `api_search`, `api_describe`, `api_reload`, `api_result_query`,
 `api_lookup`, `api_plan` and `identity`, or only `api_search`,
 `api_describe` and `api_result_query` for a caller served in group mode
 alone.
4. Call the vendor. A tool call is validated, compiled into the vendor's own
 filter dialect, sent with the credential the caller resolves to, shaped back
 into a bounded answer, and journaled.
A vendor document is never committed and never baked into the image. The
repository ships 38 compiled starter catalogs under
`catalog/` (the original Manage, RMM, Automate, CPQ,
ScreenConnect, SentinelOne, Auvik, Axcient, Huntress, Slide and AlertOps
set, plus BookStack, Sherweb, Tailscale, UniFi, TimeZest, 3CX, Twilio and
VoiceMeUp since 1.7.0). The documents they were compiled from live in the
private sources repository, `pulsatrixtechnologies/pulsatrix-sources`. The
release image copies that pack to `PXC_CATALOG_PACK` so the console add
list can import it; without the pack every add answers "starter catalog
\ is not on this gateway" (1.8.0 on GOX).

sections.title: Perspicax README.md: Why it is not a generic proxy
sections.text:
A proxy hands the model the vendor's raw surface. Perspicax curates it.
- A resource model, not a path list. Operations are folded into resources
 with verbs, so one query tool covers hundreds of GET routes and the model
 picks a resource name instead of a URL.
- A default view. A query answers with the fields that identify and describe
 each object (identity, `id`, labels, dates, the status like names, custom
 fields), not the vendor's whole page. `fields` names exactly what each item
 keeps, `fields: "*"` returns the raw object, `_format: table` returns rows
 and columns.
- Vendor knowledge where the model reads it. A guide
 (`pulsatrix-guide/1`) holds what a vendor's document does not say: which
 module holds what, the filter conventions, the time rules, per resource
 views, labels and aliases, write rules and policy lines. The connector
 renders it into each tool description, each `api_describe` card and each
 error hint, per caller and narrowed to what the caller's profile reaches,
 so a client that drops the MCP instructions loses nothing.
- Names checked before any call. A misspelled field, resource or operator
 is refused with the closest names, ranked locally without any model. A read
 argument with exactly one reading is repaired and reported in `_repaired`;
 a write is never guessed: it is refused with every problem and the whole
 corrected call in `details.suggested`.
- One filter grammar, compiled per dialect. Equality, `in`, `contains`,
 comparisons, `null` and `not_null`, and an inclusive `overlaps` window on a
 date range pair, are parsed once and compiled into `cw_conditions`,
 `s1_cursor`, `jsonapi_filter`, `plain_query`, `positional_rpc`, GraphQL
 selections, an upstream MCP tool's arguments, or the 1.7.0 dialects
 (`bracket_filter`, `unifi_filter`, `next_token`, `tql_cursor`, `odata`,
 `twilio_page`, `xml_engine`). A dialect that cannot express an operator
 refuses it by name rather than guessing.
- Handles for large results. A result above 16 KiB comes back as a handle
 with a bounded summary; `api_result_query` reads the body with JMESPath, so
 sums and counts cost one call, not one call per element.
- Read before write. An update reads the current object and sends the
 minimal JSON Patch diff. `_dry_run: true` builds the request and does not send
 it. Write tools are annotated as writes and carry a destructive hint. An
 operator may also opt in to a server-side confirmation of deletes, of
 changes to two or more records, or of every write: the first call sends
 nothing and answers a preview, and the same call with `confirm: true` after
 the user said yes runs it.
- Time in the deployment's zone. With `time_zone` set, a local time a
 caller passes is converted to the vendor's UTC, a date means that local
 day, and results show local times with their offset.
- A scope gate at call time. Every call funnels through one place that
 checks the operation against the caller's scopes before the credential and
 before the vendor.

sections.title: Perspicax: Account deletion (person erasure)
sections.text:
Status: implemented 2026-10-17 (schema 64). Loi 25 (LPRPSP art. 28):
a person's account and personal information leave Perspicax on request, and
every linked Sagax server is told to delete its own copy.

sections.title: Perspicax: Account deletion (person erasure): Console
sections.text:
One place for each action:
- An admin erases another person from that person's sheet
 (`/users/:id`, Compte, last row of the Zone sensible: « Effacer cette
 personne », lot 7 of the Cursor-style console). The row opens a step of
 the sheet that says the erasure cannot be undone (Loi 25), what goes and
 what the journal keeps; it asks whether the person's shared memory
 contributions stay, the admin's own step-up (their password and
 authenticator code, or for a passkey-only admin a sign-in of the last ten
 minutes) and the person's login typed again, and its button stays off
 until they are all there. Never on one's own sheet, never for the last
 active admin, never while viewing as someone else, and only for a person
 (a service account is deleted instead). The server's refusals read in the
 step (`step_up`, `confirm`, `last_admin`, `bound`, `rate_limited`); the
 result is a notice with the counts and a way to the admin journal, which
 holds the `user.erase` row.
- A person erases their own account in Réglages › Compte (« Supprimer
 mon compte », lot 6).

sections.title: Perspicax: Account deletion (person erasure): Recent sign-in from Sagax (2026-10-18)
sections.text:
A Sagax server holds its people's refresh tokens; a compromised one could
otherwise mint live sign-in tokens forever and erase any linked person. The
Sagax route therefore demands proof that the person themself signed in at
this Perspicax a moment ago:
- Sagax signs the person in again right before (`DELETE /api/me` answers
 `409 reauth_required` until it did): a `pulsa-bot` authorization code
 flow with `prompt=login`, `max_age=0`, `login_hint` the person's id and
 the scope `openid pulsabot:erase` (`local_oauth::ACCOUNT_ERASURE_SCOPE`),
 whose access token it keeps in memory for that one erasure. Perspicax
 keeps no browser session for its authorize page: every code is minted
 after the factors (password and authenticator code, or a passkey), so
 `prompt=login` is always honoured.
- The marker is kept only for the `pulsa-bot` client of a bound origin with
 `openid`, and only for the person the `login_hint` names (another account
 signing in, or no hint, drops it). The sign-in page shows a warning above
 the form when the request carries it ("Sagax vous demande de vous
 reconnecter pour supprimer votre compte...", `oauth-erase-notice`).
- Perspicax dates that access token: `signed_in_at` on its token record is
 the code's `auth_time`, set only by the authorization code exchange of a
 sign-in that carried the marker. An ordinary sign-in (web, phone, desktop,
 pairing), a refresh (whatever the family's `auth_time`, which its id_token
 keeps per OIDC Core 12.2), a token exchange (routine delegation) and an
 internal mint leave it at 0. Sagax never chooses it: it is Perspicax's own
 record, not a claim in the request.
- The route refuses `403 reauth_required` (`details.max_age` 300) unless
 `0 < signed_in_at <= now` and `now - signed_in_at <= 300`
 (`api::pulsabot::erase_reauth_fresh`). Nothing is erased on that refusal,
 and it is an `erase_reauth` `refused` sign-in event of the person naming
 the server (never a token), at most one a minute per server and person.
Why not the console step-up: it proves the factors to the console itself;
Sagax would have to collect the password and the authenticator code and pass
them on, which hands a compromised Sagax the very factors this guards.
Signing in again on Perspicax's own page keeps the factors there.
Refusals for every route: a non-person account (service, system, link)
`400 validation`; the last active admin `409 last_admin`; a personal key a
product an admin configured still seals `409 bound`. Nothing is erased on a
refusal, and the refusal is an `admin_audit` row `user.erase` `refused`.
Erasures run one at a time in the process (a mutex over the checks, the
memory, the keys and the transaction), so two admins erasing themselves at
once cannot both pass the last admin check; the transaction checks again
(a person an admin disabled while their own erasure ran is still erased).

sections.title: Perspicax: Account deletion (person erasure): Security review (2026-10-17, independent pass 2026-10-18)
sections.text:
- Authorization: the store re-checks inside the transaction that a person
 route erases `actor.id == id` only and that an admin route has the admin
 role and another target. The Sagax route takes the subject from the
 verified sign-in token, never from the request. Tested: the link token
 alone, a forged subject, a sign-in token as the link token, no link.
- Explicit confirmation: the login typed again (console), `{"confirm":
 true}` after Sagax's own confirmation (Sagax), plus the caller's step-up on
 both console routes (a store or vault failure there is an error, never a
 skipped factor). Irreversible actions stay behind these.
- Admin erasure is audited with the admin as actor (and their address);
 self erasure without address.
- No leaks: the audit and the delivery log name servers and counts; the
 notice token never reaches a log; refusals do not tell a person which
 product an admin wired their key into.
- Recent sign-in (2026-10-18): the Sagax route demands an interactive
 sign-in made for the erasure in the last 5 minutes (above); tested with an
 ordinary sign-in, a refreshed token, a sign-in ten minutes old, one dated
 in the future (all refused) and one four minutes old (accepted), and the
 warning on the sign-in page.
- Known limits, accepted: a compromised Sagax can still send a person to a
 sign-in made for the erasure and use it within its 5 minutes; Perspicax's
 own page warns the person before the password. `auth_time` is the time
 the code is minted, right after the factors; after a forced password
 change, a first authenticator enrolment or the profile picker (setup
 tokens of 10 minutes) it can be later than the factors themselves. A
 compromised Sagax that serves its own fake sign-in page and relays the
 password and authenticator code live gets past the warning (factor
 phishing); only a passkey resists that. A
 database backup taken before the erasure still holds the person until it
 rotates out; restoring one would bring the account back (the memory has
 tombstones, the database does not). A server unlinked while a notice is
 queued loses the notice (the row goes with the server): relinking it
 does not replay past erasures. A role or status change by another admin
 during an erasure can still make the in-transaction check refuse after
 the memory went (the person's memory and keys gone, the account kept);
 the same request, sent again, finishes. Schema 64 is additive; going
 back to 1.8.36 after it ran needs the table dropped and the version set
 back to 63 by hand, or a restore. The journal's free-text samples
 (`args_sample`, `result_sample`) are vendor data, kept and de-identified
 only by the person column.

sections.title: Perspicax: Account deletion (person erasure): The account purged notice
sections.text:
`POST /api/auth/oidc/backchannel-logout`, form
`logout_token= `: the back-channel logout token (ES256, `typ`
`logout+jwt`, `iss`, `aud` `pulsa-bot`, `iat`, `exp` +120 s, fresh `jti`,
`sub`, no `nonce`, no `sid`) whose `events` holds the back-channel logout
event and the RISC event
`https://schemas.openid.net/secevent/risc/event-type/account-purged` with
`{"subject": {"format": "iss_sub", "iss", "sub"}}`.
- Delivered only on a 2xx whose JSON says `"purged": true` (Sagax answers
 after its deletion ran). A Sagax that only knows the logout answers `{}`:
 the person is logged out there and the notice stays queued.
- Durable: `person_erasure_outbox` (migration 0064), one row per server and
 person, deleted once delivered (`pulsabot.erasure_notice.delivered`
 audit row naming the server and the attempts, never the person).
- Retries after 1 min, 5 min, 30 min, 2 h, 6 h, then every 24 h, without
 end: the row holds only the opaque id, and unlinking the server drops it.
 The sweeper runs at boot and every 60 s (`spawn_sweeper`), one pass at a
 time; a fresh `jti` per attempt; the token is never logged nor stored.
- The server that asked waits 120 s, so its own deletion runs first. Sagax
 serializes its deletion per person and makes it idempotent, so the notice
 after its own `DELETE /api/me` finds nothing more.
Sagax side: pulsatrixtechnologies/Sagax PR #713 (the erase call from
`DELETE /api/me`, the purge on the back-channel route, the principal record
anonymized rather than deleted).

sections.title: Perspicax: Account deletion (person erasure): What Perspicax deletes (`gateway::person_erasure::erase`)
sections.text:
In order, one call:
1. The checks above (`Store::erasure_target`).
2. The person's memory tier and archive (`Memory::erase_person`, tombstoned
 so a restored memory backup never brings it back; contributions to
 shared tiers are kept with their provenance unless `team_contributions:
 "remove"`; the Sagax route keeps them, decision 11). With it go the work
 registry events of their tier (and their shared ones on `remove`; kept
 ones lose the salted actor hash), their recall turns and duplicate
 hints, their writes waiting in the memory filter queue, and their id in
 the memory audit and quarantine.
3. Their personal keys (`user: ` credentials) with their bindings and
 defaults.
4. One transaction (`Store::erase_person`):
- the `users` row, and by cascade the sessions, passkeys, TOTP, avatar,
 team memberships, held profiles, personal products, user keys, SSO
 links, model keys, Sagax permission set assignments;
- deleted: sign-in events (`auth_events`), private vendor sessions,
 claims, Flow runs and leases, the data access rules written for the
 person, the thread shares to them, the email log rows to their
 addresses;
- de-identified: the request journal (`user_id`, `ip`, `user_agent` to
 NULL) and the vendor call journal (`user_id` to NULL): what was done
 on a vendor stays, not who nor from where;
- scrubbed in `admin_audit`: the before and after snapshots and the
 reason of rows about the person, the snapshots of their personal keys
 (current and deleted earlier), and the address and browser of rows
 they acted in;
- an admin viewing as the person goes back to their own account;
- one account purged notice queued per linked Sagax server;
- one `user.erase` audit row: the person's opaque id, `by`
 (`self`, `admin`, `sagax` with `server_id`) and counts only. For `self`
 and `sagax` the row carries no address nor browser.
5. Every local OAuth token of the person is revoked.
6. Their pre-gateway account file (`state/local_oauth/users/*.json`), if
 any, is removed, so `gateway init` or `import-users` cannot bring the
 account back.
7. A delivery pass starts.
The `user.erase` row changes the Sagax directory, so the linked server the
install writes the link file for is told to refresh at once.

sections.title: Perspicax: Account deletion (person erasure): Who may erase
sections.text:
| Route | Caller | Proof |
 
| `POST /api/v1/me/erase` | the person, from the console | a console session (never an API token, never while viewing as someone else), the login typed again (`confirm`), the current password when the account has one, the authenticator code when it has one, and for a passkey-only account a console sign-in of the last 10 minutes. At most 5 refused step-ups per 15 minutes (`429 rate_limited`); each refusal is an `erase_step_up` sign-in event. |
| `POST /api/v1/users/{id}/erase` | an admin, for another person | admin role, a console session (never an API token, never while viewing as someone else), the person's login typed again, the admin's own step-up (their password, their authenticator code, or a recent passkey sign-in; the same rate limit), the usual team visibility. An admin erases their own account through `/me/erase`. |
| `POST /api/v1/pulsabot/people/me/erase` | the person, from a linked Sagax (`DELETE /api/me` there) | the link token (`Authorization: Bearer`) and the person's live `pulsa-bot` sign-in access token (`X-Perspicax-Subject-Token`), body `{"confirm": true}`. The link token alone opens no person: a server can only erase the person signed in to it, while that sign-in lives. Every answer of the handler carries `X-Perspicax-Erasure: 1`, so Sagax tells this route from an older Perspicax (404 without the header). The sign-in token must come from an interactive sign-in of the last 5 minutes (see "Recent sign-in from Sagax"), else `403 reauth_required`. |

sections.title: Perspicax: Politique d'accès aux données: À quoi ça sert
sections.text:
Un administrateur peut dire qu'une personne, un compte de service (bot) ou
un rôle ne voit pas certaines entités clés (une compagnie, un board, un
site SentinelOne, un livre BookStack, un appareil Tailscale, un client
X360Recover), ni ce qui leur appartient, en lecture comme en écriture. Ou,
à l'inverse, qu'il ne voit que une liste donnée. Sans règle, rien ne
change.
La garantie ne vaut que pour le trafic qui traverse Perspicax en mode
gateway. Le connecteur standalone (mode fichiers) n'a pas d'utilisateurs et
refuse une table `[data_access_policy]` dans `config.toml`.

sections.title: Perspicax: Politique d'accès aux données: Cascade par produit
sections.text:
| Produit | Types | Ce que bloque une entité |
 
| ConnectWise PSA | compagnie, board, projet | billets, contacts, sites, configurations, ententes, opportunités, factures, temps, dépenses, projets, activités, documents ; pour un board : billets, notes, tâches, temps, rendez-vous ; pour un projet : billets de projet, phases, notes, temps |
| SentinelOne | compte, site, groupe | agents, menaces, alertes, activités, exclusions, politiques au niveau site ou groupe |
| BookStack | livre | chapitres, pages, pièces jointes, révisions, images liées (pas l'étagère en v1) |
| Tailscale | appareil, tag, utilisateur | appareils (par id, tag ou propriétaire), clés et routes d'un appareil |
| X360Recover | client | sites, appareils protégés, vaults dédiés, jobs, alertes |
Pour ConnectWise, l'appartenance à une compagnie en lecture ne compte que
le champ `company` (DAP-9). Un enregistrement lié seulement par
`billToCompany`, `shipToCompany`, `parentCompany`, `subCompany` ou
`customerCompany` reste visible. En écriture, une création ou une
modification qui pointe `billToCompany`, `shipToCompany`,
`customerCompany` ou `parentCompany` vers une compagnie bloquée (par
`id`, chemin JSON Patch, casse, forme aplatie `billToCompanyId`,
tableau en lot, `copy`/`move`) est refusée comme introuvable
(`NotFound`, jamais `policy_denied`) ; toute écriture qui nomme ces
champs par `identifier` (objet ou chemin JSON Patch) est également
refusée dès que la politique restreint `connectwise.company` (pas de
lookup : un identifier n'est jamais comparé comme un id) ;
`subCompany` n'est pas dans cette liste. La vérification ne court que
si la politique restreint `connectwise.company` (une règle board seule
ne bloque pas un téléversement multipart).

sections.title: Perspicax: Politique d'accès aux données: Ce que voit l'appelant
sections.text:

 `_policy.masked` avec le décompte.
- Accès direct à un id bloqué : même réponse qu'« introuvable » (code et
 corps), pour ne pas révéler l'existence.
- Une écriture qui nommerait une entité invisible est refusée
 (`policy_denied`) sans la nommer, ou répond « introuvable » si
 l'enregistrement visé est invisible.

1. Règles : créer, modifier, retirer une règle (sujet rôle / personne

sections.title: Perspicax: Politique d'accès aux données: Formes de règle
sections.text:
- Bloque : l'entité et ce qui lui appartient sont invisibles.
- Ne voit que : seules les entités listées de ce type restent visibles ;
 une entité créée après la règle est invisible tant qu'on ne l'ajoute pas.
La combinaison la plus restrictive gagne : union des blocages, intersection
des listes permises par type.

sections.title: Perspicax: Politique d'accès aux données: Journal
sections.text:
Chaque requête journalisée peut porter l'issue de politique (`none`,
`rewritten`, `masked`, `denied`, `not_found`), le décompte masqué et les
identifiants de règles. Jamais les données retirées.

sections.title: Perspicax: Politique d'accès aux données: Limites (à connaître)
sections.text:
- Groupes clients : hors portée v1 (voir plus haut).
- Texte libre : une note d'un billet permis qui nomme un client bloqué
 n'est pas filtrée. Ce n'est pas un DLP.
- Données déjà copiées : mémoire Perspicax, historique Sagax. Chantier
 à part.
- Trafic hors Perspicax : clé API directe, bot en solo. Hors garantie.
- BookStack : le livre seulement, pas l'étagère.
- Huntress, ConnectWise RMM, Automate et x360Cloud : non filtrés en v1.
- X360Recover : dès qu'une règle touche X360, les vaults sont refusés.
- Rendez-vous ConnectWise : seuls les types `S` et `P` sont traités ; les
 autres identifiants de type sont retirés.
- Clause `conditions` Manage au-delà de 1 800 octets : pas de réécriture à
 l'aller ; le filtre au retour reste la garantie.
- `masked: N` révèle qu'il existe N éléments hors de vue dans cette
 requête. Accepté ; seul l'accès direct est muet.

sections.title: Perspicax: Politique d'accès aux données: Qui est concerné
sections.text:
La politique s'attache à l'utilisateur (personne ou compte de service) et
au rôle (Admin, Manager, Employé), pas au profil MCP choisi. Un changement
de profil ne l'assouplit jamais. Chaque personne ou bot a ses propres
règles de compagnie et de board ; une règle d'une personne n'en réduit
jamais une autre.
- Appel humain : la personne du jeton.
- Compte de service (bot) : le compte du jeton `pxat1.`, pas la personne
 qui l'a créé.
- Conversation Sagax : la personne qui parle.
- Routine Sagax ou Flow : le propriétaire de la routine.
- Jeton échangé (RFC 8693) : l'utilisateur d'origine.

sections.title: Perspicax: Email channel
sections.text:
Date: 2026-10-02 
Role: the one sender of the connector. It mails the password reset link the
sign-in page offers under "Mot de passe oublié?", the invitation an
administrator sends a new person, a memory question (`ask_person` by email)
and a test message. It sends nothing else.
Code: `crates/gateway/src/email.rs` (providers, sealing, log),
`crates/gateway/src/api/email.rs` (routes),
`crates/local-oauth/src/password_link.rs` (the links),
`console/src/pages/admin/email.tsx` (the page).

sections.title: Perspicax: Email channel: Layout
sections.text:
Since 2026-10-19 every mail (the reset, the invitation, the test message and
a memory question of `ask_person`) is drawn by one layout,
`crates/local-oauth/src/mail.rs`: a mail is a list of blocks (paragraphs, a
quote, one action) and `Mail::render` writes both parts.
- Text part: the same sentences as before, the link on its own line, then a
 footer after `-- ` (the product, Pulsatrix Technologies Inc. and why the mail
 was sent).
- HTML part: tables and inline CSS, 600 px wide at most, the console's colours
 (`console/src/index.css`), a header with the owl tile and the product name,
 a card with a title, one primary button with the link written out under it,
 the footer with the reason, a hidden preheader, Outlook conditionals, and
 dark colours under `prefers-color-scheme: dark` (Apple Mail, Outlook for Mac
 and iOS; Gmail and Outlook.com invert the light ones). `lang` on the page,
 and on an English paragraph of a bilingual mail.
- One image: the console's opaque owl tile, `/console/icons/apple-touch-icon.png`
 on the deployment's public origin, `alt=""` since the product name stands
 beside it. No query string, nothing naming the recipient, no tracking pixel,
 no third-party image; with images off the header still reads.
- Every value is escaped where it lands; a link that is not `http(s)` is
 never clickable.
Languages are unchanged: the reset and the invitation follow the person's
locale (French or English), the test message and the question stay
bilingual. The snapshots of each mail with neutral sample values are under
`crates/gateway/tests/email_snapshots/` (`.txt` and `.html`);
`PX_UPDATE_SNAPSHOTS=1 cargo test -p gateway --test email_layout` rewrites
them.

sections.title: Perspicax: Email channel: Or from the server (defaults)
sections.text:
Read once at boot. Since 2026-10-01 these are defaults: a field saved from
the console wins, field by field, and every field stays editable there. Each
field carries a tag, Serveur or Console; a console value over a server default
offers "Revenir à la valeur du serveur", which drops the console's value. The
GOX deployment fills them from its Key Vault (`infra/README.md`, section
Courriel).
| Variable | Value |
 
| `PXC_MAIL_PROVIDER` | `twilio` or `sendgrid` (implied `twilio` when a Twilio SID and secret are set) |
| `PXC_MAIL_FROM` | the sender address |
| `PXC_MAIL_FROM_NAME` | the sender name |
| `PXC_MAIL_TWILIO_SID` | the Twilio API key SID |
| `PXC_MAIL_TWILIO_SECRET_FILE` or `PXC_MAIL_TWILIO_SECRET` | the Twilio secret, from a file (preferred) or the value |
| `PXC_MAIL_SENDGRID_KEY_FILE` or `PXC_MAIL_SENDGRID_KEY` | the SendGrid key, the same way |
Upgrade from 1.7.0 and older: a save then wrote every field, the server's ones
too, and the server won. On the first boot after the upgrade the connector
drops, once, every console row of a field the environment sets (those rows had
no effect), so nothing changes until someone saves; the marker
`email_console_first` in `settings` makes it run once.
A secret from the environment is never sealed into the store and never logged.
`PXC_TWILIO_EMAIL_URL` and `PXC_SENDGRID_URL` point the providers at a local
test sink and are honored only for a loopback `http://` URL.

sections.title: Perspicax: Email channel: Providers
sections.text:
| Provider | Endpoint | Credentials |
 
| Twilio Email API (default) | `POST https://comms.twilio.com/v1/Emails` | API key SID (`SK...`) and secret, HTTP Basic |
| Twilio SendGrid | `POST https://api.sendgrid.com/v3/mail/send` | API key (`SG....`), Bearer |
Every message carries a text part and an HTML part (Twilio refuses a content
with only `text`), both from the branded layout below. The provider's reference of an accepted message is kept in
the delivery log: Twilio's `operationId`, SendGrid's `X-Message-Id`. SMTP is not
offered: a provider over HTTP needs no new dependency, and nothing asked for
SMTP.
The sender must be verified at the provider. Twilio and SendGrid both refuse
a sender address whose domain is not authenticated (or, on SendGrid, a single
sender that is not verified). Twilio answers `400` with "The from.address domain
'x' is not valid or authorized."; the console shows that sentence as the test
result. Verify the domain first (`pulsatrix.ca` for `noreply@pulsatrix.ca`).

sections.title: Perspicax: Email channel: Routes
sections.text:
`PUT /api/v1/settings/email` is a patch: a field left out is kept, `null`
clears the console's value (the server's default applies again; for a secret,
the sealed one is removed) and a value is saved from the console. A blank
secret keeps the stored one; `clear_twilio_secret` and `clear_sendgrid_key`
(the 1.6.2 shape) still mean `null`. A save that would leave an active
provider without a sender address, or Twilio without a SID, is refused whole
and audited as refused.
| Route | Role |
 
| `GET /api/v1/settings/email` | admin |
| `PUT /api/v1/settings/email` | admin |
| `POST /api/v1/settings/email/test` | admin |
| `GET /api/v1/settings/email/log` | admin |
| `POST /api/v1/users/{id}/invite` | admin |
| `GET`, `POST /oauth/password/forgot` | public (the sign-in page) |
| `GET`, `POST /oauth/password/reset` | public (the link) |

sections.title: Perspicax: Email channel: Secrets
sections.text:
The Twilio secret and the SendGrid key are sealed in the vault (`email_secrets`,
AAD `(name, "email")`), re-sealed by `gateway rotate-vault`. The settings view
answers only `twilio_secret_configured`, `sendgrid_key_configured` and
`api_key_configured`, and in `fields` each field's `source` (`console`,
`server`, `none`), `server_default` and, for a plain field only,
`server_value`; a provider's error text is scrubbed of the secret before
it reaches the answer, the delivery log or a log line; the audit row of a save
names which secret was replaced or cleared, never its value. The delivery log
keeps the recipient, the subject, the outcome and the provider reference, never
a body (a body carries a live link), and is pruned with the journals
(`retention_days_journal`).

sections.title: Perspicax: Email channel: Set it up in the console
sections.text:
Système > Courriel (`/console/settings/email`), admin only. The page head
carries two actions, Envoyer un test and Configurer. The page shows a status
card: the state (Prêt, Incomplet, En échec when the last attempt failed,
Désactivé), the provider, the sender as the recipient reads it
(`Perspicax `), the last accepted send and the last
error in words; under it, the delivery log, which lists every attempt,
filters by state, and opens one row's details in the right sheet (J and K
walk the rows).
Configurer opens the settings in the right sheet (`?config=1`), one tab each:
1. Fournisseur: Twilio Email API (offered first), SendGrid or Désactivé.
2. Identifiants: only the chosen provider's. The Twilio API key SID (`SK...`,
 not a secret) shows masked (`SK9f…64c3`) until "Afficher le SID". A secret
 shows "Configurée" and a Remplacer button; it is write only and no response
 ever carries it back.
3. Expéditeur: an address on the verified domain, for example
 `noreply@pulsatrix.ca`, and an optional name, with the From line previewed.
Enregistrer, in the sheet's footer, waits for a change; the form checks the
address, the SID and the key the provider needs before it saves, and opens
the first tab with an error. Closing with a change asks first.
"Envoyer un test" opens a dialog addressed to the signed-in administrator:
"Message accepté par le fournisseur (référence ...)" means the provider took
it; a refusal is said in words ("Nom ou adresse d'expéditeur refusé par
Twilio", "Clé d'API invalide ou révoquée", ...) with the provider's own
message under "Message du fournisseur".

sections.title: Perspicax: Email channel: What goes out, and when
sections.text:
- Reset: the sign-in page's "Mot de passe oublié?" asks for the login. The
 answer is the same whether the account exists or not, is disabled, or is a
 service account, and the mail leaves on its own task, so neither the
 answer nor its time tells. A link goes only to an active person who
 already has a second factor (TOTP or a passkey) and an address: a
 disabled, service or factor-less account is a no-op (no mail). A link
 sets a password, and a password alone never signs anyone in. Limits: 5
 requests per 15 minutes per client, 3 mails per hour per account (the
 rest are dropped silently), 10 link submissions per 15 minutes per
 client. With no channel configured the page keeps its hint (ask your
 administrator).
- Invitation: `POST /api/v1/users/{id}/invite`, from the person's sheet
 (Sécurité > Invitation par courriel) or the create sheet (an email, then
 "Envoyer une invitation par courriel plutôt qu'un mot de passe temporaire").
 The first sign-in then enrolls the second factor. The route answers 400
 when the account is a service account, is disabled, or has no address
 (`this account is disabled`, `a service account never signs in`,
 `this person has no email address`); 409 when local OAuth is off or the
 channel is not configured. One `user.invite` audit row whatever the
 provider answers, refusals included.
- A link is `/oauth/password/reset?token=...`, signed with HMAC-SHA256 under
 `state/local_oauth/password_link.key` over the purpose, the account, the
 expiry and the account's current password hash: it works once (setting the
 password changes the hash), any other password change voids it, and it
 expires after 30 minutes (reset) or 72 hours (invitation). A still-valid
 link of an account that is later disabled, deleted or turned into a
 service account answers `account inactive` and sets nothing. Setting the
 password through a link revokes the account's OAuth tokens and console
 sessions; the second factor stays.

sections.title: Perspicax: Flow actions on a Perspicax host (lots B.1 and B.3, slices 1 and 2): 1. Configure the host
sections.text:
Environment of the connector (read at boot; the trust root never comes from
the console):
| Variable | Meaning |
 
| `PXC_FLOW_TENANT_SLUG` | The one Flow tenant this host serves (`acme`, `[a-z0-9-]+`). Without it nothing is staged (`flow_not_configured`). |
| `PXC_FLOW_ALLOWED_SIGNERS` | The OpenSSH `allowed_signers` file of the pack signatures; default ` /flow/allowed_signers`. A line must name the namespace: `flow@pulsatrix namespaces="pulsatrix-flow-pack" ssh-ed25519 AAAA...`. `cert-authority` lines are ignored. |
| `PXC_FLOW_TEST_ACTIONS` | `1` on a test or lab host only: the pack's `test-*` actions become visible. Never on a production host. |
| `PXC_FLOW_PYTHON` | The interpreter, when not `/usr/bin/python3` (a development Mac). |
| `PXC_FLOW_GUARD` | The server guard (section 6.1): `off` (default), `shadow` (logs what it would refuse, refuses nothing) or `enforce`. Any other value is `enforce`. |
The image ships `python3` and `tzdata` (Debian trixie, 3.13). On Linux the
runner refuses to start without Landlock's file system rules
(`SandboxPolicy::Required`); a macOS development host runs it best effort.
Files under ` /flow/`: `packs/ /` (unpacked read only, the
active pack and the four most recent others), `home/` (`PX_FLOW_HOME`, the
only folder the runner may write: the Flow journal v2 under
`home/logs/ / .jsonl`, written by the pack's `serve`).

sections.title: Perspicax: Flow actions on a Perspicax host (lots B.1 and B.3, slices 1 and 2): 2. Build a pack (in `pulsatrix-flow`)
sections.text:
The pack only comes from tags; it is never committed. ` ` gets
`pack.tar` (with `MANIFEST.json` at its root), `MANIFEST.json` and
`MANIFEST.json.sig`; the digest `sha256: ` of `pack.tar` is printed.

sections.title: Perspicax: Flow actions on a Perspicax host (lots B.1 and B.3, slices 1 and 2): 3. Upload, activate, roll back (admin)
sections.text:
The admin token comes from the secret store by variable name, never typed in
clear. With `PX_ADMIN_TOKEN` set from the store:
 
Staging checks, before anything is written: the SSHSIG of the manifest
against `allowed_signers` (`pack_signature_invalid`), every file against the
manifest (`pack_manifest_mismatch`), the entries (only files under
`product/` and `tenant/`, no link, no `..`: `pack_entry_invalid`), the
tenant (`pack_tenant_foreign`) and `requires_host` (`pack_requires_host`).
Staging never moves the active pack. Activation bumps the registry version:
the runtime reloads and `tools/list_changed` goes out; an action already
running finishes on the pack it started with. Audit rows: `flow.stage`,
`flow.activate`, `flow.rollback` (refusals as `refused`).
A pack that is not active is removed with `DELETE
/api/v1/flow/packs/sha256: ` (204, its row and its folder; the active
pack answers 409 `flow_pack_active`; audit `flow.delete`). `GET
/api/v1/flow/host` reads the host settings back (tenant slug, allowed
signers file and principals, host version, runner sandbox `required` or
`best_effort`, test actions); nothing there is editable.
The console does the same on the Flow page (`/console/flow`, admins): the
packs with their signer, build time, size and state, staging from local
files, activate, roll back, delete, the profile links of section 4, the
host settings read only and a dry run of one action with its render.

sections.title: Perspicax: Flow actions on a Perspicax host (lots B.1 and B.3, slices 1 and 2): 4. Link a profile
sections.text:
`role` is `interactive` (a person: batch confirmation) or `routine` (action
writes only under its live lease, section 6.1). A routine profile names the one routine it runs
and who runs it, for `flow_run` (section 6.2):
`{"flow": {"tenant": "acme", "role": "routine", "routine": "weekday-project-health-watch", "executor": "claude-code-cloud"}}`
(`routine` is `[a-z0-9-]+` and only on a routine profile; `executor` is
`claude-code`, `claude-code-cloud`, `cowork` or `manual`, only with a
routine, and the pack's routine wins over it, section 6.2).
`{"flow": null}` unlinks. The tenant comes from
the profile, never from a call. A caller whose profiles are linked to two
different tenants is refused (`flow_binding_ambiguous`): connect with one
profile (`/mcp?profile= `).
### From the host, without an admin session
The connector binary does the same as sections 3 and 4 over the same store
(same checks, same audit rows, actor `system`), for a host where no admin
token is at hand (the GOX VM: `infra/README.md`, "Packs Flow"):
 
`bind` refuses a tenant other than `PXC_FLOW_TENANT_SLUG`. The running
server reads the active pack and the profile links at boot: restart the
connector after a change made this way (the API path reloads by itself).

sections.title: Perspicax: Flow actions on a Perspicax host (lots B.1 and B.3, slices 1 and 2): 5. Use it
sections.text:
A linked caller is listed two tools while a pack is active, in every service
mode: `flow` (`{command: "catalog"}`, `{command: "describe", args: {name}}`)
and `flow_action` (`{name, params, _dry_run?, confirm?}`, or `{resume:
{run_id, choice}, confirm?}` after a `choice_needed`, section 5.1).
| `status` | Meaning |
 
| `done` | The final render (`markdown`, `json`, `silent`); `writes` lists each write. |
| `dry_run` | Real reads, every write sent with `_dry_run: true`, nothing changed. |
| `needs_confirmation` | `preview` lists each planned write (target, field, before, after) and the targets already done; call again with the same name and params and `confirm: true` after the user said yes (10 minutes, once, by the same caller). A plan that changed meanwhile is a new preview and nothing is sent. |
| `stop` | A tenant fact is not set (`field`); nothing was written after the stop. |
| `blocked` | `reason` says why and the answer says what was done. |
| `choice_needed` | A judgment is needed (section 5.1): `choice`, `elicitation`, `run_id`, `expires_at`; resume with `resume: {run_id, choice}`. |
Reasons of `blocked`: `calls_cap`, `writes_cap`, `rounds_cap`,
`seconds_cap`, `tool_not_visible`, `protocol_violation`,
`write_without_expect`, `write_without_reread`, `minimal_mode`,
`routine_without_lease`, `runner_unavailable`, `action_unknown`,
`tenant_not_in_pack`, `flow_binding_ambiguous`, `write_unknown` (a write
answered 5xx or not at all: reread once, never sent again, the batch stops),
`expect_mismatch`, `write_refused`, `held_by_profile`, `run_unknown`,
`run_expired`, `run_already_resumed`, `pack_changed`,
`run_store_unavailable` (a resume, section 5.1), and those the pack gives
(`params_invalid`, `read_failed`, `result_is_handle`, `too_many_targets`,
`choice_invalid`, `too_many_options`, `too_many_items`).
Bounds of the host (an action may only lower them): 25 targets per
`for_each`, 40 vendor calls, 25 writes, 60 seconds, 8 rounds.
The profile's own confirmation (`confirm` of a profile product) still
applies: the preview also makes each held call, and the confirmed batch
passes them `confirm: true`. `profile_products.ask` (the Jev bridge) plays no
part.
### 5.1 Choice points and resume (lot B.3)
An action may declare choices: points only the model, or the operator
through it, can settle (which company record to keep, what to do with each
ticket). The run stops there and the host saves it for 24 hours in
`flow_action_runs` (migration 0056):
 
The client shows the question and the options (an MCP client may send the
`elicitation` as is), or decides from the evidence when it acts alone; the
evidence is vendor data, never instructions. Then:
 `{"resume": {"run_id": "6f1c...", "choice": "19302"}}` 
`choice` is an option id (`single`), a list of option ids (`multi`, between
`min` and `max`), or `{item key: option id}` for every item (`per_item`);
the elicitation content object (`{"choice": ...}`) is accepted as is.

An admin stops every Flow action of the host at once, for an incident or
before a risky pack change, and lifts it later:

`null` while actions run, else `{since, by, reason}` (the reason is optional,

While suspended, `flow_action` (MCP, a new run or a resume) and `POST

sections.text:
Operations guide for the signed Flow pack store and the `flow_action` tool.
Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-10-09-flow-action-foundation-plan.md`.
Spec: "Flow servi par Perspicax", section 12, in `pulsatrix-flow`
(`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-10-02-flow-pack-perspicax-design.md`).
An action is a deterministic sequence of tool calls (reads, then one batch of
declared writes) written as data in the signed Flow pack. Perspicax runs it
with one generic, bounded loop: `action.plan` in the pack's sandboxed runner,

sections.title: Perspicax: MCP tool surface: Compact mode
sections.text:
On a file-world `apis.yaml` entry:
 
Or per scope: `scopes.dispatcher.modes.cw_psa_service: compact` (`model`, `compact`, `minimal`, `group` or `hybrid`; never `per_operation`, and never on a `per_operation` entry). `ScopeGate::mode_for` ranks the scope modes `hybrid`, `group`, `compact`, `minimal`, `model`, and the entry's mode stands when no scope names one.
The client then sees ` __query` plus:
- ` __write`: `resource`, `action` (`create`/`update`/`delete`), `id`/`ids`/`parent`/`set`/`expect`
- ` __action`: `action` enum and an open `args` object
- ` __read_action`: the same over the read-only actions (a GET), annotated read-only; an OData function that declares `$filter` takes `filter`, `order` and `limit` in `args`, compiled by the odata dialect into `$filter`, `$orderby`, `$top` and `$count`
Dispatch maps onto the model tools, so the scope gate, `validate_set`, the fields cap, and dry run stay the same. Enums are narrowed to what the caller can reach.
A guide with `serve.fold_model: "compact"` serves a caller resolved to `model` the compact view of its API (the SentinelOne starter guide does this).

sections.title: Perspicax: MCP tool surface: Confirmation (opt-in)
sections.text:
By default nothing changes: no connector argument is required to execute a write, and the client's permission panel, `readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint` and `_dry_run` are the write gate (spec D15). An operator may opt in per `apis.yaml` entry, per group member, per scope, or per gateway profile product (the Confirmation checkboxes of the profile editor):
 
| Kind | Holds |
 
| `delete` | every delete (a write tool delete, a DELETE operation) |
| `bulk` | a write naming two or more `ids`; an operation whose path ends in `/bulk`, whose body is an array of two or more records, or that takes two or more `ids` or a `filter` |
| `writes` | every non-GET, which includes the other two |
`bulk` also holds a mass change sent one record at a time. The Qwen evaluation saw a model close two tickets with two single-record updates, once in three episodes of its mass-close trap (`evals/small-model/reports/2026-09-26-qwen3.6.md`, finding h08), which a rule judged per call never held. So, under a set naming `bulk` (and not `writes`, which holds every call anyway), an update or a delete of one record through a write tool (model, compact, group write, or an update recipe in hybrid) is held when the same MCP session sent an update or a delete of another record of the same resource of the same API in the last ten minutes (`call::confirm::SESSION_WINDOW`). The rules:
- The session is the transport `Mcp-Session-Id`, else the journal's session id (`mcp: : `), so a long conversation that crosses an hour starts a new count.
- Records are counted per API and resource (`cw_psa_service` tickets and notes count apart) and by id and parent: the same ticket updated twice is one record and is never held for it.
- A write counts once the vendor took it (`ok` and a record sent); a held preview, a dry run and an update that changes nothing do not count. A create never counts and is never held by this rule.
- The held call answers the preview below with `confirm.kind` `bulk` and `confirm.count` the records of that resource the session changed, this one included; its sentence names how many other records the session changed. `confirm: true` sends it as for any held call, and every later record of that resource in the window is held again.
- A call inside a parent request is outside the rule: a Flow batch has its own batch confirmation, and an `api_plan` step writes only as a dry run. Action and `per_operation` tools stay judged one call at a time.
- An empty confirm set changes nothing (DEC-4), and a set without `bulk` never counts anything.
A held call sends nothing to the vendor. It answers, not as an error:
 
The same call repeated with `confirm: true` by the same caller within ten minutes of its preview runs it. `confirm: true` on a call no preview preceded is held like a first call. `_dry_run: true` is never held.

sections.title: Perspicax: MCP tool surface: ConnectWise identities
sections.text: Who a ConnectWise Manage write may name is a setting of the caller's profile, one per category (console: profile, tab ConnectWise, "Identités et usurpation"; API `PUT /api/v1/profiles/{id}/cw-identity`): `note_author` (a note's member, createdBy, enteredBy), `time_member`, `schedule_member`, `expense_member`, `task_member`, `assignment` (owner, resources, assignTo, assignedBy, sales reps, manager), `audit_fields` (closedBy, enteredBy, updatedBy of other records), each `self_or_bot`, `self`, `bot` or `any`; `note_contact` and `contact` (tickets, activities, opportunities, orders, projects), each `existing`, `any` or `forbidden`. Defaults: a note is written as the API member (member left out) or as your own member, never as a contact; everything else is free. Your own member is matched from the e-mail of your Perspicax account against `officeEmail` or `primaryEmail`; the API member is the one the connector saw ConnectWise write a record as. The check is in the call funnel (`crates/connector-core/src/call/cw_identity.rs`), so it holds for every write tool, mode, recipe, per-operation tool, `api_plan` step and `flow_action`, and for `_dry_run`. A refusal is `policy_denied` with `details.reason: "cw_identity"`, the `category`, the `setting` and the `field`, before the vendor.

sections.title: Perspicax: MCP tool surface: Filter grammar
sections.text:
Parsed once in `dialect/mod.rs`, then compiled per dialect.
| Spelling | Meaning |
 
| `{ "status.name": "New" }` | Equality |
| `{ "id": { "in": [1, 2] } }` | In |
| `{ "summary": { "contains": "outage" } }` | Contains (dialect-dependent) |
| `{ "dateEntered": { "gte": "2026-09-01" } }` | Comparison |
| `{ "resources": { "eq": null } }` or `{ "null": true }` | Is null |
| `{ "owner": { "ne": null } }` or `{ "not_null": true }` | Is not null |
| `{ "date": { "overlaps": ["2026-09-10T00:00:00Z", "2026-09-10T23:59:59Z"] } }` | Inclusive window on a date-range pair |
| `{ "date": { "gte": "2026-09-10T00:00:00Z" } }` | A comparison on a range name: `gte`, `gt`, `lt`, `lte` apply to the start field; `between [a, b]` and a date-only `eq` become `overlaps` over whole days |
Conditions combine with AND only; `or`, `and`, `not` and `conditions` are refused as field names.
A bare `{ "field": null }` is refused (`filter. is null`): an argument that renders as JSON null must never become a silent is-null. Spell `{ "eq": null }` when you mean is-null.
`overlaps` takes two date-time strings (`from` no later than `to`). A date-only bound is refused. The pair is derived at runtime from the element schema (`dateStart`/`dateEnd` or `startX`/`endX`) or from `resources. .date_ranges` in the notes file. Expansion is `start <= to` and `end >= from` before any dialect compiles.
| Dialect | null / not_null | overlaps | Notes |
 
| `cw_conditions` | yes (`field=null` / `field!=null`) | yes | Nested fields with dots |
| `s1_cursor` | refused | yes (query `__gte` / `__lte`) | Body filters on SentinelOne actions refuse overlaps |
| `jsonapi_filter` | refused | refused | Equality and `in` only |
| `bracket_filter` | refused | refused | Laravel listings (BookStack): `filter[field]` and `filter[field:ne|gt|gte|lt|lte|like]` (`contains` is `like %value%`), `in` refused; `sort=+field` / `-field`; paging by `count` and `offset` (or `page` when the operation has no `offset`); a declared plain parameter (`query` of `/api/search`) rides as is, equality only; `{ data, total }` |
| `unifi_filter` | yes (`field.isNull()` / `field.isNotNull()`) | yes (`ge` / `le`) | UniFi Network Integration API: one `filter` expression, `field.eq(v)`, `ne`, `in(a, b)`, `gt`, `ge`, `lt`, `le`, several joined by `and(...)`; `contains` is `like('*value*')` (the vendor's own `contains` tests a SET property, not reachable); a string in single quotes, a number, a boolean, an ISO 8601 date or a UUID bare (the property type deciding when the element schema declares it: a STRING property quoted whatever the value looks like); a key that is not a property path refused; a value with `'` or `\` refused (no documented escape); a declared plain parameter rides as is, equality only; no order; paging by `limit` (at most 200) and `offset`, `next` the absolute offset of the rows after the page (a short page, or a list with no `limit`, advances by what came back); `{ offset, limit, count, totalCount, data }` |

sections.title: Perspicax: MCP tool surface: Group and hybrid
sections.text:
A plain catalog id also belongs to a group when it came from one split import (`--split ... prefix=cw_psa_`) or when two or more served catalogs share one source document and a ` _`. The members of one group served grouped must share a filter dialect.
- ` __query` takes `resource` over every member's resources, then the usual `filter`, `fields`, `order`, `limit`, `cursor`, `id`, `parent`, `include`, `expand`. A name one member serves is bare (`members`); a name several serve carries its module (`service.tickets`, `project.tickets`); a bare name that collides is refused naming the choices. `include` takes the same spellings; `expand` also follows a reference into a sibling member (a ticket's `company`).
- ` __write` and ` __action` take the compact write and action arguments with the group spelling; ` __action` routes to the write and the read-only actions of the members alike, read-only only when every one of them is. A profile with no write grant sees no ` __write`.
- The guide's `hide` globs (`*_info`, `*_count`, ...) drop reference-noise names from the advertised enums only; a hidden name is still dispatched, described and searched.
